summary: Psalm 125 compares those who trust in Yahweh to Mount Zion, stable and enduring. It pictures Yahweh surrounding his people as mountains surround Jerusalem, then asks for good to come to the upright while warning that those who turn aside will be led away with evildoers.
whyItMatters: This short Song of Ascents gives a pilgrimage-sized statement of trust: God’s people are threatened, but not abandoned. It also holds together confidence, petition, warning, and a final prayer for Israel’s peace.

context.author: Anonymous within the Psalter; Psalms is a multi-author anthology formed over time.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping community, with later Jewish and Christian communities also praying and interpreting these poems.
context.date: Individual psalms may come from different periods, from the monarchy through the postexilic era; one date for the whole Psalter would be misleading.
context.setting: Book V of Psalms, within the Songs of Ascents, a group of short psalms associated with going up toward Jerusalem.
context.literaryForm: Compressed Hebrew poetry and prayer, using image, contrast, petition, and a closing blessing.

outline.heading: Trust Like Mount Zion
outline.note: Those who trust in Yahweh are compared to Mount Zion, unmoved and lasting.

outline.heading: Yahweh Around His People
outline.note: Jerusalem’s surrounding mountains become an image for Yahweh’s surrounding care.

outline.heading: Wicked Rule Limited
outline.note: The psalm says wicked authority will not remain over the righteous, so the righteous are not pushed toward evil.

outline.heading: Prayer for the Upright
outline.note: The speaker asks Yahweh to do good to the good and upright in heart.

outline.heading: Warning and Peace
outline.note: Those who turn to crooked ways are grouped with workers of iniquity, and the psalm ends, 'Peace be on Israel.'

keyVerses.text: A Song of Ascents. Those who trust in Yahweh are as Mount Zion, which can’t be moved, but remains forever.
keyVerses.why: This opening gives the psalm its central image: trust in Yahweh is described through Zion’s stability.

keyVerses.text: As the mountains surround Jerusalem, so Yahweh surrounds his people from this time forward and forever more.
keyVerses.why: The verse expands the Zion image into a picture of Yahweh’s protective nearness to his people.

keyVerses.text: For the scepter of wickedness won’t remain over the allotment of the righteous, so that the righteous won’t use their hands to do evil.
keyVerses.why: This explains why the psalm can speak confidently: wicked rule is real, but it is not portrayed as permanent.

keyVerses.text: But as for those who turn away to their crooked ways, Yahweh will lead them away with the workers of iniquity. Peace be on Israel.
keyVerses.why: The ending contrasts the fate of the crooked with a final wish for Israel’s peace.

questions.question: What is a 'Song of Ascents'?
questions.answer: The phrase appears in verse 1 as part of the psalm’s heading. The Songs of Ascents belong to Book V’s pilgrimage material, but the exact original performance setting should not be overstated from the heading alone.

questions.question: Why compare trusting people to Mount Zion?
questions.answer: Verse 1 says those who trust in Yahweh are like Mount Zion, 'which can’t be moved, but remains forever.' The point in the verse is stability, not that trusting people never suffer or never feel afraid.

questions.question: What does Jerusalem add to the image?
questions.answer: Verse 2 moves from Mount Zion to the mountains around Jerusalem. The surrounding landscape becomes a poetic image for Yahweh surrounding his people 'from this time forward and forever more.'

questions.question: Does verse 3 mean wicked rulers never have power?
questions.answer: No. Verse 3 assumes a 'scepter of wickedness' can be over 'the allotment of the righteous.' Its claim is that such rule 'won’t remain,' so the pressure on the righteous is real but not final in the psalm’s hope.

questions.question: What is the danger named at the end of verse 3?
questions.answer: The verse says wicked rule will not remain 'so that the righteous won’t use their hands to do evil.' The concern is that prolonged unjust power could draw the righteous into wrongdoing; the psalm asks readers to see pressure and moral danger together.

questions.question: Who are 'those who are upright in their hearts'?
questions.answer: Verse 4 pairs 'those who are good' with 'those who are upright in their hearts.' Within this chapter, that phrase describes the people for whom the speaker asks Yahweh to do good.

questions.question: Why does the psalm ask Yahweh to do good if it already says Yahweh surrounds his people?
questions.answer: The psalm contains both confidence and petition. Verse 2 declares Yahweh surrounds his people, while verse 4 still asks, 'Do good, Yahweh,' showing that trust can speak as prayer rather than only as a conclusion.

questions.question: Who are the people who 'turn away to their crooked ways'?
questions.answer: Verse 5 contrasts them with the good and upright people named in verse 4. The chapter does not give their names or a specific historical episode; it describes a moral direction and says Yahweh will lead them away with 'the workers of iniquity.'

questions.question: What does 'Peace be on Israel' do at the end?
questions.answer: The final sentence turns the psalm outward to Israel as a whole. After warning about crooked ways, it closes with a compact blessing or prayer for peace on the community.

glossary.def: The divine name used in this translation. In this psalm, Yahweh is the one trusted, the one who surrounds his people, the one asked to do good, and the one who leads away those who turn aside.
The mountain image in verse 1 for what cannot be moved. The psalm uses it to describe the stability of those who trust in Yahweh.
The city named in verse 2. Its surrounding mountains provide the psalm’s image for Yahweh surrounding his people.
The phrase in verse 3 for wicked rule or authority. The psalm says it will not remain over the righteous.
The phrase in verse 5 for the path of those who turn away. The psalm contrasts them with the good and upright in heart.
